text.p: Italian debt markets rebounded from the day's lows by the end of trade after a day wracked by rumours and a flood of economic information.

The government unveiled its three-year economic plan (Dpef) and confirmed the 1998 budget would aim for 25 trillion lire of budget deficit-trimming measures, with 10 trillion in new revenue and 15 trillion in spending cuts.

This all disappointed some market players who said the document failed to address structural spending reforms but it did not surprise others who said it was about as much as the coalition could manage given political constraints.

The June Btp future on LIFFE, which goes off the board next week, was 27 basis points up at 128.99 having ducked all the way down to support at 128.06 earlier on rumours, since denied, that rating agencies were reconsidering Italy's rating.
The rumour flung the BTP-Bund spread out to 151 basis points before it was cleared up. It then recovered to 141 bps.

That panic over, out came Italy's economic goals for 1998 to 2000. GDP growth is targeted at 2.0 percent, inflation at 1.8 pct and the deficit/GDP ratio at 2.8 pct next year. Earlier, preliminary data showed GDP shrank in the first quarter of 1997, down 0.5 percent year on year and 0.3 percent on the quarter.

"The Dpef is not having a huge effect. The key elements like the 1998 budget amount are as per expectations - 25 trillion and some moves on pensions but that's a subject that has to be tackled separately," said Luca Jellinek at Paribas in London.

With the Dpef out of the way, players said the market was watching ballot results in France and the row over Bonn's plans of how to account for EMU and its effect on progress towards a European single currency. Generally all bonds were judged a bit shaky but Italy was seen as benefiting if EMU was broadened.
Brokers said rate cut hopes were returning as the lira stabilised -- but this was unlikely for several days or weeks.
